screens.title: What is Chaos Engineering?
screens.narratorSegment: Chaos Engineering is the disciplined practice of experimenting on a system to identify weaknesses and build confidence that it will remain healthy under turbulent conditions. At the center of each experiment is a measurable steady state — a set of metrics or business signals that indicate normal operation such as low error rates, acceptable latency, or successful logins. You begin by stating a hypothesis: for example, 'users can log in while one web server instance fails.' That hypothesis shapes what you will measure before, during, and after injecting a fault. The purpose is not to find bugs alone; it's to discover unknown failure modes that only appear when components interact under stress. A common misconception is that chaos engineering is reckless; in fact, it is careful and controlled. You minimize blast radius, automate stop conditions, and run in production-like environments where results are most meaningful. A clear test example is injecting network latency to a database tier to observe whether request retries, timeouts, and fallback mechanisms maintain the steady state. The concrete takeaway is this: when you can state a steady state, measure it, and test it under fault, you move from assumptions to verified resilience. What observable metric would you pick as your steady state for your most critical user journey?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › What is Chaos Engineering?
Definition
Hypothesis-driven experiments to reveal resilience gaps
Key attributes to remember:
  • • Steady state: measurable indicator of health such as low 5XX errors or stable latency.
  • • Hypothesis: a testable claim about how the steady state should behave under fault.
  • • Controlled fault: realistic events like instance termination or CPU stress.
  • • Observation: automated monitoring to compare before/during/after behavior.
Key Takeaway
A clear hypothesis and steady state make experiments useful and actionable.
Concrete Example
Hypothesis: The application will maintain low 5XX rates even when one web server instance fails. Fault: terminate one instance in the Auto Scaling group. Observe: ALB 5XX count and latency. If the steady state breaks, investigate health checks or scaling delays.
Common Misconception
People sometimes treat chaos as random destruction. Real experiments are deliberate, small, and instrumented to learn.
Why measure
Metrics turn assumptions into verifiable facts.
Why start small
Small blast radius reduces risk and focuses learning.
Reflection
Pick one customer-facing steady state you can measure this week. How would terminating a single instance affect it?

screens.title: Core Principles of Chaos Engineering
screens.narratorSegment: Chaos Engineering rests on a concise set of principles that shape safe, informative experiments. First, start with a hypothesis: choose a steady state and assert that it will hold despite a specific fault. This keeps experiments measurable and focused. Second, vary real-world events: inject faults that mirror realistic failure modes such as network latency, C P U saturation, or instance termination. Varying the event lets you discover different failure pathways. Third, prefer production-like environments: experiments in a staging environment often miss scale and configuration differences; running in production-like systems makes findings applicable. Fourth, automate experiments and observations so you can run them reliably and repeatedly; automation also enables quick rollback and consistent data collection. Fifth, minimize blast radius: begin small, limit affected resources, and have a rollback plan. Finally, include stop conditions — automated alarms that halt the experiment if critical metrics cross thresholds. A typical process flow is: define hypothesis, design an experiment template, set targets and stop conditions, run the experiment, observe and compare results to the hypothesis, then iterate with fixes and re-run. A common mistake is skipping the hypothesis and treating the experiment as a checklist; always make your expected steady state explicit so observations lead to concrete improvements.

screens.title: Chaos Experiments vs Traditional Testing
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between traditional testing and chaos experiments helps you pick the right tool for resilience work. Traditional tests — unit, integration, and load tests — verify that components and well-known flows work as designed. They are deterministic and aim to catch regressions or performance issues under expected conditions. Chaos Engineering, by contrast, intentionally introduces realistic unexpected failures to validate that the system maintains its steady state under adverse conditions. The purpose is not to prove correctness of a single component but to reveal coupling, timing issues, and emergent behavior at scale. For example, a load test might show that auto-scaling launches new instances under traffic. A chaos experiment could simulate the auto-scaling failing to launch instances and reveal whether health checks and fallback circuits keep the system operating. A frequent misconception is that chaos replaces testing — it does not. Use chaos to complement tests: tests reduce obvious defects, while chaos exposes unknown failure modes. A practical rule is to keep tests deterministic and use chaos for stochastic, scenario-based validation. When you combine both, you get higher confidence that systems will behave under both expected and unexpected conditions.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Experiments vs Tests
Traditional Testing
Unit tests, integration tests, and load tests check correctness and performance under expected conditions. They are deterministic, automated, and used to prevent regressions.
  • • Focus: correctness and performance.
  • • Outcome: pass/fail for specific scenarios.
  • • Strength: reproducible and fast feedback.
Chaos Experiments
Introduce faults like instance termination or network latency to validate the system maintains steady state under adverse conditions. They reveal emergent behaviors and timing issues at scale.
  • • Focus: resilience and emergent failure modes.
  • • Outcome: validated confidence or identification of weaknesses.
  • • Strength: uncovers problems tests do not capture.
Complementary
Use tests for correctness, experiments for resilience.
Scale Matters
Run experiments in production-like environments to reveal scale-dependent issues.
Iterate
When a steady state breaks, fix and re-run the experiment to validate the improvement.

screens.title: AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) Overview
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Fault Injection Simulator is a managed service that structures chaos experiments into repeatable templates. An experiment template encapsulates the actions you will inject, the targets those actions affect, and the stop conditions that automatically halt the experiment if critical alarms fire. Actions are concrete faults such as terminating EC2 instances, injecting C P U stress, or adding network latency. Targets define which resources to affect: you can specify resource ARNs, or use selection modes like a percentage of instances with specific tags. Stop conditions are typically CloudWatch alarms monitoring metrics such as error rates or status-check failures; they act as automated circuit breakers. The template also references an IAM role with least privilege so FIS can perform the actions. This structure makes experiments auditable and reusable. A frequent practical question is how to pick targets; use tags and selection modes to scope the blast radius precisely. Another operational tip is to keep stop conditions conservative for production-like tests so experiments halt before user impact grows. FIS encourages automation and iteration — once you create a template, you can run it repeatedly, analyze, and improve your architecture based on observed outcomes.

keyIdea.title: FIS anatomy
keyIdea.text: Experiment templates combine actions, targets, stop conditions, and an IAM role so experiments are repeatable and safe.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › AWS FIS Overview
FIS Building Blocks
Actions: Faults like terminate-instances or CPU stress.
Targets: Resources to affect; by tags, ARNs, or selection modes like PERCENTAGE.
Stop Conditions: CloudWatch alarms that stop the experiment automatically.
Role: An IAM role with least privilege for FIS to execute actions.
Pro tip
Use tags and percentage selection to control blast radius precisely and make templates reusable across environments.
Small Template Example
{
  "description": "Terminate 25% of WebApp instances",
  "targets": { "WebAppInstances": { "resourceType": "aws:ec2:instance", "selectionMode": "PERCENTAGE(25)", "parameters": { "filters": [{"path": "Tags.Name", "values": ["WebAppInstance"]}, {"path": "State.Name", "values": ["running"]}] } } },
  "actions": { "TerminateInstances": { "actionId": "aws:ec2:terminate-instances", "parameters": { "instanceIds": "${WebAppInstances}" }, "targets": { "Instances": "WebAppInstances" } } },
  "stopConditions": [{ "source": "aws:cloudwatch:alarm", "value": "arn:aws:cloudwatch:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:alarm:WebApp5XXAlarm" }],
  "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/FISExperimentRole"
}
This conceptual JSON shows targets, actions, and stop conditions. Use IAM roles with least privilege when creating templates.
Key Takeaway

FIS templates make chaos experiments repeatable, scoped, and safe by design.

Check
Can you name an alarm that would be a good stop condition for your service?

screens.title: FIS Experiment Template Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simplified FIS experiment template to see how actions, targets, and stop conditions come together. The description names the experiment. Targets list resource selectors; for example, a target named WebAppInstances can use resourceType aws:ec2:instance with selectionMode PERCENTAGE(25) and filters on tags and state. Actions reference an actionId such as aws:ec2:terminate-instances and map targets into parameters that specify which instances to terminate. Stop conditions reference CloudWatch alarm ARNs; if a monitored metric crosses a threshold, FIS automatically stops the experiment. Finally, roleArn points to an IAM role, FISExperimentRole, that grants FIS the permissions to act. A common misconception is that the template itself causes harm — templates only describe an experiment until you start it. Treat the template as a plan you can review, test in a dev environment, and iterate. When authoring templates, keep selectionMode conservative, use tags for precise targeting, and choose alarms that reflect critical application health. After an experiment runs, review logs and metrics to determine if the steady state held and what corrective actions are needed. screens.title: Designing a Terminate-Instances Experiment
screens.narratorSegment: This guided plan mirrors the hands-on activity in the chapter. Start by ensuring you have multiple EC2 instances tagged as WebAppInstance in an Auto Scaling Group and an IAM instance profile for management. Next, create a CloudWatch alarm to act as a stop condition — for example, monitor StatusCheckFailed_Instance or an ALB 5XX metric and set the threshold so the alarm fires early in an outage scenario. Then create an IAM role for FIS with the AWSFISServiceRolePolicy and least-privilege permissions. In FIS, create an experiment template: set a target that selects PERCENTAGE(50) or PERCENTAGE(25) of instances with the appropriate tags, add an action aws:ec2:terminate-instances targeting that group, and attach the CloudWatch alarm as the stop condition. Before running, notify teams and verify monitoring dashboards are active. Start the experiment, monitor EC2 and FIS consoles, and watch the alarm — if it fires, the experiment stops automatically. After the run, analyze whether the steady state held: did auto-scaling replace instances quickly enough? Were health checks configured correctly? This structured approach reduces risk and yields actionable results. Step-by-step Plan

screens.title: Safety and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Safety is the most important consideration when running chaos experiments. Start small: target non-critical components or a small percentage of instances and expand scope only after verifying behavior. Define a clear blast radius by using tags and selection modes to precisely identify which resources are affected. Implement robust stop conditions by creating CloudWatch alarms on critical metrics such as 5XX error rates or status-check failures; these alarms act as automatic brakes if the experiment begins to harm users. Communicate with stakeholders and on-call teams before running experiments so everyone knows where to look and how to respond. Monitor heavily during experiments using CloudWatch, tracing, and application logs to collect actionable data. Always have a rollback plan and test it ahead of time; do not rely on manual fixes in the middle of an active experiment. Finally, use IAM roles with least privilege for FIS so the experiment cannot perform unintended actions. A common mistake is running aggressive experiments without adequate monitoring or stop conditions — this increases the risk of an uncontrolled outage. Treat safety controls as integral to the experiment, not optional extras.

screens.title: Interpreting Results and Improving Resilience
screens.narratorSegment: Interpreting the results of a chaos experiment is as important as running the experiment correctly. Start by comparing observed metrics to your hypothesis and steady state. If the steady state held, you validated a resilience assumption and gained confidence. If it broke, you have actionable evidence of a weakness. Analyze logs, traces, scaling events, and health-check behavior to find root causes — perhaps auto-scaling took too long, health checks were overly aggressive, or a dependency failed to degrade gracefully. Design corrective actions: adjust scaling thresholds, improve health checks, add retries or circuit breakers, or increase capacity. After implementing fixes, re-run the same experiment to validate the improvement. This iterate-and-verify loop converts a discovered weakness into a proven fix. A misconception is treating a single experiment as conclusive; instead, use repeated experiments to gain statistical confidence. Document outcomes and update runbooks so operations teams can respond faster. The final aim is not to eliminate all failures, which is impossible, but to reduce unexpected user impact by pre-validating resilience mechanisms. In practical terms, compare observations to hypotheses, fix root causes, and re-run experiments. screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes can turn a useful experiment into a risky or uninformative one. First, running aggressive experiments without adequate stop conditions or monitoring is dangerous; alarms are your automated safety net. Second, skipping the hypothesis makes results hard to interpret — always state what steady state you expect and why. Third, using staging environments that do not reflect production scale or configuration can produce misleading results; when possible, run experiments in production-like environments. Fourth, granting overly broad IAM permissions to FIS increases risk; use least-privilege roles. Fifth, failing to communicate with teams and on-call operators can delay response and increase impact; schedule experiments and notify stakeholders. Finally, treating a single experiment as definitive is a mistake — use repeated experiments and post-fix validation to gain confidence. To avoid these pitfalls, design conservative experiments first, automate stop conditions, align observations with hypotheses, and iterate on fixes with re-testing. That way, experiments become reliable instruments for improving resilience rather than sources of risk. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore why intentionally introducing faults helps you build more reliable systems. Chaos Engineering is a disciplined approach: you form a hypothesis about a system’s steady state, inject a controlled fault, observe what happens, and learn. This matters because real outages rarely look like textbook failures; systems behave badly in complex ways when multiple components interact. You will see how experiments differ from unit tests and load tests, how the AWS Fault Injection Simulator provides the building blocks for safe experiments, and how to use stop conditions and blast radius limits to protect production-like environments. I will also guide you through a concrete example where a percentage of web tier instances are terminated while a CloudWatch alarm acts as an automated circuit breaker. By the end, you will understand not just mechanics but the mindset: experiments are hypotheses to validate resilience, not destructive tests for their own sake. Notice common safety practices and what an iterative experiment, analyze, and improve loop looks like. Ask yourself: what steady state in your application would you measure first to know it’s still healthy?

These objectives map to practical capabilities you will use when designing resilient systems. First, you will learn the core principles of Chaos Engineering so you can form testable hypotheses about your system’s steady state and recognize meaningful observables such as error rates and latency. Second, you will be able to explain how chaos experiments differ from standard testing, understanding when an experiment reveals resilience gaps instead of functional bugs. Third, you will learn to use AWS Fault Injection Simulator to automate controlled experiments, including composing actions, targets, and stop conditions. Finally, you will practice designing experiments with limited blast radius, selecting appropriate stop conditions, and interpreting results to drive improvements. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you know when you’ve demonstrated the skill in a lab or production-like environment.

This second objectives slide focuses on measurable outcomes from the hands-on lab. You will be able to design an FIS experiment template that targets a percentage of EC2 instances, add a CloudWatch alarm as a stop condition, and run an experiment while observing instance termination and its impact. You will learn to analyze results by comparing observed behavior to your hypothesis and determining root causes when the steady state breaks. You will also practice safety procedures such as creating an IAM role with least privilege, tagging resources for precise targeting, and cleaning up resources after the experiment. These outcomes ensure you can run experiments responsibly in production-like environments and iterate to improve resilience. Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes means design, run, observe, and analyze an fis experiment while enforcing safety and least-privilege practices.. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chaos Engineering is the disciplined practice of experimenting on a system to identify weaknesses and build confidence that it will remain healthy under turbulent conditions. At the center of each experiment is a measurable steady state — a set of metrics or business signals that indicate normal operation such as low error rates, acceptable latency, or successful logins. You begin by stating a hypothesis: for example, 'users can log in while one web server instance fails.' That hypothesis shapes what you will measure before, during, and after injecting a fault. The purpose is not to find bugs alone; it's to discover unknown failure modes that only appear when components interact under stress. A common misconception is that chaos engineering is reckless; in fact, it is careful and controlled. You minimize blast radius, automate stop conditions, and run in production-like environments where results are most meaningful. A clear test example is injecting network latency to a database tier to observe whether request retries, timeouts, and fallback mechanisms maintain the steady state. The concrete takeaway is this: when you can state a steady state, measure it, and test it under fault, you move from assumptions to verified resilience. What observable metric would you pick as your steady state for your most critical user journey?

Chaos Engineering rests on a concise set of principles that shape safe, informative experiments. First, start with a hypothesis: choose a steady state and assert that it will hold despite a specific fault. This keeps experiments measurable and focused. Second, vary real-world events: inject faults that mirror realistic failure modes such as network latency, C P U saturation, or instance termination. Varying the event lets you discover different failure pathways. Third, prefer production-like environments: experiments in a staging environment often miss scale and configuration differences; running in production-like systems makes findings applicable. Fourth, automate experiments and observations so you can run them reliably and repeatedly; automation also enables quick rollback and consistent data collection. Fifth, minimize blast radius: begin small, limit affected resources, and have a rollback plan. Finally, include stop conditions — automated alarms that halt the experiment if critical metrics cross thresholds. A typical process flow is: define hypothesis, design an experiment template, set targets and stop conditions, run the experiment, observe and compare results to the hypothesis, then iterate with fixes and re-run. A common mistake is skipping the hypothesis and treating the experiment as a checklist; always make your expected steady state explicit so observations lead to concrete improvements.

Understanding the difference between traditional testing and chaos experiments helps you pick the right tool for resilience work. Traditional tests — unit, integration, and load tests — verify that components and well-known flows work as designed. They are deterministic and aim to catch regressions or performance issues under expected conditions. Chaos Engineering, by contrast, intentionally introduces realistic unexpected failures to validate that the system maintains its steady state under adverse conditions. The purpose is not to prove correctness of a single component but to reveal coupling, timing issues, and emergent behavior at scale. For example, a load test might show that auto-scaling launches new instances under traffic. A chaos experiment could simulate the auto-scaling failing to launch instances and reveal whether health checks and fallback circuits keep the system operating. A frequent misconception is that chaos replaces testing — it does not. Use chaos to complement tests: tests reduce obvious defects, while chaos exposes unknown failure modes. A practical rule is to keep tests deterministic and use chaos for stochastic, scenario-based validation. When you combine both, you get higher confidence that systems will behave under both expected and unexpected conditions.

AWS Fault Injection Simulator is a managed service that structures chaos experiments into repeatable templates. An experiment template encapsulates the actions you will inject, the targets those actions affect, and the stop conditions that automatically halt the experiment if critical alarms fire. Actions are concrete faults such as terminating EC2 instances, injecting C P U stress, or adding network latency. Targets define which resources to affect: you can specify resource ARNs, or use selection modes like a percentage of instances with specific tags. Stop conditions are typically CloudWatch alarms monitoring metrics such as error rates or status-check failures; they act as automated circuit breakers. The template also references an IAM role with least privilege so FIS can perform the actions. This structure makes experiments auditable and reusable. A frequent practical question is how to pick targets; use tags and selection modes to scope the blast radius precisely. Another operational tip is to keep stop conditions conservative for production-like tests so experiments halt before user impact grows. FIS encourages automation and iteration — once you create a template, you can run it repeatedly, analyze, and improve your architecture based on observed outcomes.

Targets list resource selectors; for example, a target named WebAppInstances can use resourceType aws:ec2:instance with selectionMode PERCENTAGE(25) and filters on tags and state. Actions reference an actionId such as aws:ec2:terminate-instances and map targets into parameters that specify which instances to terminate. Stop conditions reference CloudWatch alarm ARNs; if a monitored metric crosses a threshold, FIS automatically stops the experiment. Finally, roleArn points to an IAM role, FISExperimentRole, that grants FIS the permissions to act. Several common mistakes can turn a useful experiment into a risky or uninformative one. First, running aggressive experiments without adequate stop conditions or monitoring is dangerous; alarms are your automated safety net. Second, skipping the hypothesis makes results hard to interpret — always state what steady state you expect and why. Third, using staging environments that do not reflect production scale or configuration can produce misleading results; when possible, run experiments in production-like environments. Fourth, granting overly broad IAM permissions to FIS increases risk; use least-privilege roles. Fifth, failing to communicate with teams and on-call operators can delay response and increase impact; schedule experiments and notify stakeholders. Finally, treating a single experiment as definitive is a mistake — use repeated experiments and post-fix validation to gain confidence. To avoid these pitfalls, design conservative experiments first, automate stop conditions, align observations with hypotheses, and iterate on fixes with re-testing. That way, experiments become reliable instruments for improving resilience rather than sources of risk.
